extracted.intended_audience: general public, patient advocates, policymakers, and legal/medical communities interested in gene-patenting policy
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the legal, policy, and public-health criteria for whether human genes (and related genomic sequences) should be patentable, using AMP v. Myriad and its consequences as the focal example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent-ineligibility: laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The page cites "150 years of legal precedent forbidding patents on laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas," and notes the Supreme Court agreed with that principle in AMP v. Myriad, invalidating patents on two human genes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use established precedent excluding laws of nature/natural phenomena/abstract ideas from patentability as a primary legal test when evaluating gene-related patent claims; AMP v. Myriad is treated as a controlling example where the Court invalidated gene patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolation does not confer patentability for naturally occurring DNA
rubrics_metrics.description: The article explains Myriad obtained patents because it was first to "isolate" BRCA1/BRCA2 (remove them from the body and cell) but the litigation argued human genes are products of nature "even when 'isolated'."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims that rely solely on 'isolation' of naturally occurring sequences skeptically: removing a sequence from a human body, without other qualifying modification or inventiveness, should not make it patent-eligible under the reasoning highlighted in AMP v. Myriad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents should not authorize private control of fundamental human material
rubrics_metrics.description: ACLU's position: it "opposes patenting that would authorize private entities to control access to something as fundamental to humanity as our genes."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing patent proposals or grants, consider whether the claimed monopoly would give private actors control over access to genetic information or material that stakeholders consider a basic human right; such control is presented as a disqualifying or harmful outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access and equity impacts on patients and underserved populations
rubrics_metrics.description: The article discusses concrete harms: Myriad's patents allowed it to "exercise a monopoly... shutting down other labs from offering testing or second opinions and increasing the price to thousands of dollars per test," making testing inaccessible and disproportionately affecting underserved and underrepresented populations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate gene-related patents by their anticipated effects on cost, availability of second opinions, and disproportionate impacts on marginalized groups; equitable access to testing and care is presented as an important metric of whether patents are appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects on innovation, competition, and scientific collaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Interviewees state gene patents "prevented the scientific community from working together to develop novel diagnostics and treatments," while the post-Myriad environment saw rapid growth ("over 160,000 clinically orderable genetic tests" in 2021).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether a patent will spur or hinder innovation and competition: if exclusivity blocks widespread research, standardization, or multiplex testing, that weighs against granting broad gene patents; empirical post-Myriad growth is cited as evidence that non-patentability can expand innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact on laboratory standards, testing quality, and clinical practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Nussbaum argues that removing gene patents "enables competition, and improves laboratory practices for genetic testing through standardizing next-generation-sequencing methods, variant classification, reporting, and counseling."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess patents by their downstream effects on laboratory method standardization, variant interpretation practices, and the quality/consistency of clinical reporting and counseling; patents that impede these improvements are presented negatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-health and emergency-response considerations (viral genomes/exemplars)
rubrics_metrics.description: Weck uses the COVID-19 example: had someone patented the SARS-CoV-2 genomic sequence, "we could have had as few as a single test, and perhaps even available from only one laboratory," which would have hampered testing capacity during the pandemic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating patent policies for genetic material, include public-health scenarios: patents that could constrain rapid scale-up of diagnostics in outbreaks are flagged as particularly harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy and legislative risk to judicial precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: The article warns that certain Congressmembers "have supported legislation to restore patenting of laws of nature and abstract ideas, including human genes," which "would overturn decades of Supreme Court precedent."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess proposed changes to patent law not only by current judicial precedent but also by legislative risk: potential statutes that would reauthorize patents on natural laws/genes should be evaluated for their systemic effects on innovation, access, and existing protections.
